classification.difficultyReason: Infer boundary lengths after cutting and overlapping a rectangular strip, then calculate the composite perimeter.

inlines.text: Vince has a rectangular piece of scrap paper. He decides to cut a quarter of the rectangle off, and places it over the remaining paper to make a new shape, as shown.
What is the perimeter of this new shape?

spec.description: An upright rectangle with an external 8 cm top dimension and 16 cm right dimension has a vertical dashed cut at three quarters of its width. A right-pointing arrow leads to an L-shaped arrangement: the cut strip lies horizontally over the remaining rectangle at its top, projecting right. Preserve the horizontal placement seam and external dimensions of 16 cm across the complete top and 16 cm along the complete height.
spec.mathematics: The original rectangle is 8 by 16. Its quarter-width strip is 2 by 16; the remaining rectangle is 6 by 16. The strip overlaps the top 2 units of the remaining rectangle. The final outline has vertices (0,0), (6,0), (6,14), (16,14), (16,16), (0,16). These coordinates are derived from the printed dimensions and quarter cut; inferred lengths are not labelled in the question figure.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source-supplied dimensions are visible. No perimeter or inferred boundary lengths appear.

answer.worked:
The strip overlaps the top of the remaining rectangle. Add the six outside edges; the placement seam is internal.

$$\begin{align*}
\text{Strip width} &= 8\div4=2\text{ cm}\\
\text{Remaining width} &= 8-2=6\text{ cm}\\
\text{Inner horizontal edge} &= 16-6=10\text{ cm}\\
\text{Inner vertical edge} &= 16-2=14\text{ cm}\\
P &= 16+2+10+14+6+16\\
P &= 64\text{ cm}
\end{align*}$$
